title: Understanding HTTP Methods
learning_outcomes: Explain how understanding http methods affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from method semantics to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on understanding http methods in http methods and operation semantics. You will connect method semantics to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding HTTP Methods matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying method semantics deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 39 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 39: Method semantics → Safe and unsafe methods → Idempotent and non-idempotent operations → Method selection principles.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Choose a method according to intended semantics, including safety and idempotency—not merely the desired database operation. In this lesson, treat “Understanding HTTP Methods” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to connect
items: Match the method to standardized semantics

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Understanding HTTP Methods
content_blocks.code:
GET    /v1/tasks/42       # retrieve; safe and idempotent
POST   /v1/tasks          # submit a new task
PUT    /v1/tasks/42       # replace the target representation
PATCH  /v1/tasks/42       # apply a partial update
DELETE /v1/tasks/42       # request removal
content_blocks.expected_output: Each request method has defined semantics. The server must not hide unrelated state changes inside a nominally safe GET request.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Method semantics”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Safe and unsafe methods” and “Method selection principles”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Method names are a contract: model safe reads, replacements, patches, and deletes deliberately. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating understanding http methods. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Method semantics” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Understanding HTTP Methods with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating understanding http methods as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: Choose a method according to intended semantics, including safety and idempotency—not merely the desired database operation. In this lesson, treat “Understanding HTTP Methods” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 40: The GET Method.
